content_voiceover: This slide shows the morphologic hallmarks of sideroblastic anemia. On electron microscopy, iron-laden mitochondria cluster around the nucleus. On Prussian blue stain, this appears as a ring sideroblast, iron granules encircling at least one-third of the nuclear circumference, the diagnostic finding for sideroblastic anemia and MDS with ring sideroblasts. On peripheral smear, severe disease shows a dimorphic red cell population, one normal and one hypochromic microcytic; mild disease shows uniform hypochromic microcytic cells that can mimic iron deficiency anemia. You may also see siderocytes, mature red cells retaining iron granules, and Pappenheimer bodies, irregular basophilic iron inclusions on Wright stain, distinct from the single round Howell-Jolly bodies of nuclear remnants. The unifying lab pattern is excess total body iron, elevated serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation, the opposite of iron deficiency anemia, and the key discriminator on boards.
keypoints: Ring sideroblast = iron in >=1/3 of nuclear circumference (Prussian blue)
Diagnostic for sideroblastic anemia and MDS-RS
Mild SA can mimic iron deficiency (hypochromic microcytic)
SA labs: ↑ serum iron, ↑ ferritin, ↑ transferrin sat (opposite of IDA)
Pappenheimer bodies (iron, irregular) vs Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear, round)
keypoint_voiceover: The must-know finding is the ring sideroblast, iron granules encircling at least one-third of the nucleus on Prussian blue stain, diagnostic for sideroblastic anemia and MDS with ring sideroblasts. Mild disease looks hypochromic and microcytic, so it can be confused with iron deficiency, but the labs are opposite, with elevated serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation. Also distinguish Pappenheimer bodies, irregular iron inclusions, from Howell-Jolly bodies, which are round nuclear remnants.
